interactions.label: A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis delivers an effective dose of approximately

params.question: A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis delivers an effective dose of approximately 8–10 millisieverts. How does this compare to the effective dose from a single chest X-ray?

answers.text: It is roughly equivalent to 2–3 chest X-rays

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A chest X-ray delivers only ~0.02 mSv. The CT dose is 400–500 times higher, not 2–3 times. This massive gap is precisely why CT is never the default first investigation.

answers.text: It is roughly 50 times the dose of a chest X-ray

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: At ~0.02 mSv per chest X-ray, 50 times would be only 1 mSv — far below the 8–10 mSv range of an abdominal CT. The true ratio is approximately 400–500 fold.

answers.text: It is roughly 400–500 times the dose of a chest X-ray

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A chest X-ray delivers ~0.02 mSv while an abdominal CT delivers ~8–10 mSv — a 400–500× difference. This is why CT requires clinical justification and is not the default first investigation.

answers.text: It is roughly 10 times the dose of a chest X-ray

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ten times 0.02 mSv is only 0.2 mSv — far below the 8–10 mSv of an abdominal CT. The actual ratio is approximately 400–500 fold.

overallFeedback.feedback: The chest X-ray delivers ~0.02 mSv and abdominal CT delivers ~8–10 mSv — roughly 400–500 times more. This gap is why every CT request must be clinically justified.
Exactly. The enormous dose difference between a plain chest X-ray and an abdominal CT underpins the ALARA principle: never default to CT when a lower-dose modality can answer the clinical question.

interactions.label: Gadolinium-based contrast agents must be avoided in patients with a documented a

params.question: Gadolinium-based contrast agents must be avoided in patients with a documented allergy to iodinated contrast.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Gadolinium contains no iodine. The two contrast families are chemically distinct: iodinated agents are used in CT and fluoroscopy, gadolinium agents in MRI. A documented allergy to iodinated contrast does not predict a reaction to gadolinium-based agents.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Gadolinium contains no iodine. The two contrast families — iodinated agents (used in CT and fluoroscopy) and gadolinium agents (used in MRI) — are chemically distinct and do not cross-react. A documented iodinated contrast allergy does not predict a gadolinium reaction.

params.question: A 45-year-old factory worker who grinds metal daily is referred for an MRI of the knee. Which additional investigation is mandatory before this patient enters the MRI scanner?

answers.text: Serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Renal function screening is essential before administering gadolinium contrast, but the critical safety concern for a metal grinder is potential ferromagnetic intra-ocular foreign bodies, which require a different investigation.

answers.text: Orbital X-ray to rule out metallic intra-ocular foreign bodies

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Any history of metal grinding or welding mandates an orbital X-ray before MRI. Ferromagnetic fragments in the eye can become projectiles in the strong magnetic field, causing devastating ocular injury.
An ECG is relevant when screening for cardiac devices such as non-MR-conditional pacemakers. The immediate concern with a metal grinder is ferromagnetic eye fragments, requiring an orbital X-ray.
A coagulation profile is relevant for invasive procedures, not routine MRI. The critical pre-MRI screen for a metal grinder is an orbital X-ray to exclude ferromagnetic intra-ocular foreign bodies.

overallFeedback.feedback: Any history of metal grinding or welding requires an orbital X-ray before MRI. Ferromagnetic fragments become projectiles in the magnetic field. This is part of the MRI safety screen applied before every scan.

Correct. The MRI safety screen specifically flags metal grinding and welding as indications for an orbital X-ray. This is one of the three pre-imaging safety screens — radiation, contrast, and MRI — that every requesting clinician must run.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old man presents with fever, localised tibial pain, and raised inflamm

params.question: A 30-year-old man presents with fever, localised tibial pain, and raised inflammatory markers. Osteomyelitis is suspected. Which imaging modality is the most appropriate first-line investigation?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Plain X-ray produces a two-dimensional projection image. It shows established cortical destruction but lacks the sensitivity to detect the early bone marrow oedema and soft-tissue changes that characterise early osteomyelitis.
CT provides excellent cross-sectional imaging of cortical bone but misses the early marrow oedema and soft-tissue changes that MRI reveals. For suspected osteomyelitis, MRI is the superior modality.
MRI reveals early bone marrow oedema and soft-tissue changes in osteomyelitis that CT will miss. Its superior soft-tissue contrast makes it the first-line modality for suspected bone infection.

Bone scintigraphy is sensitive but lacks specificity — it cannot reliably distinguish infection from fracture healing, tumour, or other causes of increased bone turnover. MRI provides both sensitivity and anatomical detail.

overallFeedback.feedback: For osteomyelitis, MRI is the first-line modality because it reveals early bone marrow oedema and soft-tissue changes that CT will miss. This follows the two-question selection framework: identify the pathology type, then match to the modality with the best diagnostic yield.

Correct. Apply the two-question framework: the problem is infection (osteomyelitis) in a limb; MRI's superior soft-tissue contrast reveals marrow and periosteal changes that CT and X-ray will miss at this early stage.

interactions.label: A pregnant woman is brought to casualty after a road traffic accident with suspe

params.question: A pregnant woman is brought to casualty after a road traffic accident with suspected abdominal injury. Applying the integrated reasoning chain of physics, screening, and selection, which imaging study should be performed first?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT delivers ~8–10 mSv of ionising radiation. In pregnancy, the fetus is the most radiosensitive subject. A non-ionising modality — the FAST scan — answers the immediate trauma question without radiation exposure.

An abdominal X-ray uses ionising radiation and provides limited information about solid-organ injury in trauma. The FAST scan answers the clinical question without any ionising exposure and can be done at the bedside.

Ultrasound uses sound waves, not ionising radiation — safe for mother and fetus. The FAST scan matches the trauma mechanism and the pregnancy. Physics, screening, and selection converge on one answer.

MRI avoids ionising radiation but is time-consuming and unsuited for rapid assessment in acute trauma. The FAST scan provides immediate bedside evaluation of free intra-peritoneal fluid within minutes.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct answer is the FAST scan. Ultrasound uses sound waves (no ionising radiation), passes all screening checks in pregnancy, and the selection framework identifies it as first-line for trauma. Physics, screening, and selection run as one chain.

Correct. The physics tells you ultrasound is non-ionising and safe for the fetus. The screening confirms no contraindication. The selection framework identifies FAST as first-line for trauma in pregnancy. Three steps, one integrated act.
